items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: One I hired on the street in my neighborhood, because she had just become a social worker and she was a mom in my kid’s class, and I adored her.

ctx.x: Right, your stuff was in drawer back in the flood in New Orleans. So I would have to call up the social workers. At that point, we now had two more social workers that we hired instantly. One I hired on the street in my neighborhood, because she had just become a social worker and she was a mom in my kid’s class, and I adored her. I just said, “We need you” and she said yes. She’s been with us ten years, Alisa Hafkin. So if one person needs their apartment, now you have to call up the landlord of the place they…

give a month’s rent and a month’s security for everyone who needed it. But you don’t want to tell that to a landlord, because he’s going to figure after the first month he’s screwed. We know that they’ll be working, because we’re going to give them work in the Jazz in the Schools. But there’s a lot you don’t want to explain. So I would call up the potential landlord. They’d tell me they found a place, it looks great, “I told the landlord you’re my reference.” So I’d call up and that’s when I’d go into the British…

items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026
items.q: I will hand them over of course to our head angel Alisa at the Jazz Foundation, you know, who is head of the social work department

ctx.x: Okay, because I know you have other questions. But I ended up, so after this was sort of taken out of my hands it was like the beginning of the pandemic and there was such a need – I was having ten musicians a day calling me so of course I want you to know that musicians still call me and I still counsel and I’m still there for them, and now if it becomes issues with money I’ll counsel them and soothe the soul but then I will hand them over of course to our head angel Alisa at the Jazz Foundation, you know, who…

way. But I was like left without purpose. It wasn’t a job that I was giving up, it was a way of life that I had designed to fit all my greatest neuroses and that’s how it worked you know. My need to care for the suffering, my purpose in life, what gave me joy in this world. That’s what gives me happiness. So it’s purely selfish on my part. So Ukraine had just had Russia invade and I think it was five or six months into the war there, the invasion there, and I was so tired of hearing about it I decided I was going…
